newsitem.title: USA: Dollar shakes off Hashimoto comments to end higher.
newsitem.headline: Dollar shakes off Hashimoto comments to end higher.

text.p: The dollar rose on Tuesday along with stocks and bonds in relief after Japanese officials played down fears sparked on Monday that Japan would pare its massive holdings of U.S. government securities.

On Monday, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto triggered a huge drop in the Dow Jones industrial average and depressed U.S. Treasuries by saying Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its Treasury holdings and boost its gold reserves due to volatility in foreign exchange rates.

"It would be both a short-term and a long-term negative if those events came to pass, but obviously I don't think anybody seriously thinks the Japanese are going to declare that type of economic retaliation on us," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president at Signet Bank in Richmond, Va. "People have basically discounted it at this point."

Japan's Ministry of Finance said on Tuesday that Japan would continue to cooperate with the United States to stabilise exchange rates and that Hashimoto regretted that his intentions had not been accurately portrayed.
Hashimoto spoke in Japanese to a group of investors at Columbia University in New York and some confusion surrounded the accuracy of the English-language translation of his remarks.

The dollar gained on Tuesday to 114.83 yen from 114.74 at Monday's close and to 1.7232 marks from 1.7175. Traders said the dollar faces tough resistance above 115 yen, where offers from Japanese trust banks lurk to sell dollars for yen.

The market was focused on Tuesday night's expected release of the Bank of Japan's quarterly tankan survey of corporate sentiment, seen as an important clue to the central bank's monetary policy. The survey is set for release at 7:50 p.m. EDT/2350 GMT.
It is expected to show weak business sentiment. The key manufacturers' index for the second quarter was forecast at -0.8 against a 2.0 reading previously.

"Everyone is waiting for this number out of Japan. If it is -2.0 or less, people will buy dollars on that and we would break 115 yen," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president and trader at Sakura Bank Ltd. in New York.
Stealing the spotlight was the British pound, which fell from a 59-month peak of 2.8818 marks after a Goldman Sachs & Co. research report said sterling was overvalued by 15 percent.
The pound drifted below support at $1.6655 but partially recovered by the close to end at $1.6685 compared with $1.6717 at Monday's close and $1.6700 at the open.
The dollar received a small lift after the Conference Board said U.S. consumer confidence reached a 28-year high in June, with its index at 129.6 compared from a revised 127.9 in May.

Also bolstering the dollar was San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank President Robert Parry's remark that he sees no clear sign of an end to the U.S. economic recovery, which is currently in its seventh year.
Parry added that he sees robust U.S. growth and well-behaved inflation and that, despite Hashimoto's remarks, there should be no significant drop in overall demand for U.S. securities.
In other trading, the dollar gained to 1.4385 Swiss francs from 1.4305 on Monday and to Canadian $1.3908 from C$1.3887.
